sections.heading: 2 Tensor attention reformulation
sections.text: Our strategy is to rewrite the multi-head attention formalism as tensor-valued operations, which allows us to define flexible low-rank training methods for various types of attention formalisms. Let X ∈ ℝ N × d model X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\rm{model}}} be an embedded sequence of N N tokens with embedding dimension d model d_{\rm{model}} . Standard MHA splits the d model × d model d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{model}} key, query, and value matrices across n H {n_{\rm{H}}} heads by a column splitting: W Q = [ W 1 Q , ⋯ , W n H Q ] , W K = [ W 1 K , ⋯ , W n H K ] , W V = [ W 1 V , ⋯ , W n H V ] , \displaystyle\begin{split}W^{\rm{Q}}&=[W^{\rm{Q}}_{1},\cdots,W^{\rm{Q}}_{n_{\rm{H}}}],\\ W^{\rm{K}}&=[W^{\rm{K}}_{1},\cdots,W^{\rm{K}}_{n_{\rm{H}}}],\\ W^{\rm{V}}&=[W^{\rm{V}}_{1},\cdots,W^{\rm{V}}_{n_{\rm{H}}}],\end{split} where W i Q , W i K , W i V ∈ ℝ d model × d H W^{\rm{Q}}_{i},W^{\rm{K}}_{i},W^{\rm{V}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{H}}} are the query, key, and value heads, and d H := d model / n H d_{\rm{H}}:=d_{\rm{model}}/{n_{\rm{H}}} is the head dimension. Using a slightly refined definition of a head, which includes the output projection matrix W i O ∈ ℝ d H × d model W^{\rm{O}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{H}}\times d_{\rm{model}}} , we have head i = Attention ​ ( X ​ W i Q , X ​ W i K , X ​ W i V ) ​ W i O = σ ⁡ ( X ​ W i Q ​ ( X ​ W i K ) ⊤ d H ) ​ X ​ W i V ​ W i O . \displaystyle\begin{aligned} \text{head}_{i}=\,&\text{Attention}(XW^{\rm{Q}}_{i},XW^{\rm{K}}_{i},XW^{\rm{V}}_{i})W^{\rm{O}}_{i}\\ =\,&\sigma\left(\frac{XW^{\rm{Q}}_{i}(XW^{\rm{K}}_{i})^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\rm{H}}}}\right)XW^{\rm{V}}_{i}W^{\rm{O}}_{i}.\end{aligned} (1) where σ \sigma is the row-wise softmax activation. Additionally, head i ∈ ℝ N × d model \text{head}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\rm{model}}} which lets us rewrite the MHA formalism as MHA ​ ( X ) = ∑ i = 1 n H head i . \displaystyle\text{MHA}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm{H}}}\text{head}_{i}\,. We propose to reformulate the attention formalism to allow for the construction of more memory efficient representations. Our derivation is based on two key observations: First, the key and query matrices form a rank d H d_{\rm{H}} factorization of the pre-softmax weight W i := W i Q ​ W i K , ⊤ ∈ ℝ d model × d model W_{i}:=W^{\rm{Q}}_{i}W_{i}^{{\rm K},\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{model}}} per head i i . Analogously value and output matrices form a rank d H d_{\rm{H}} factorization of the post-softmax weight W ~ i := W i V ​ W i O ∈ ℝ d model × d model \widetilde{W}_{i}:=W^{\rm{V}}_{i}W^{\rm{O}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{model}}} . Then, the MHA mechanism formally becomes MHA ​ ( X ) = ∑ i = 1 n H σ ⁡ ( X ​ W i ​ X ⊤ d H ) ​ X ​ W ~ i . \displaystyle\text{MHA}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm{H}}}\sigma\left(\frac{XW_{i}X^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\rm{H}}}}\right)X\widetilde{W}_{i}\,. Thus, MHA is able to encode low-rank behavior only per-head but not across heads. Second, the per-head matrices W i W_{i} and W ~ i \widetilde{W}_{i} can be collected as a tensor by stacking over all head indices, i.e., 𝒲 \displaystyle\mathcal{W} = ( W i ) i = 1 n H ∈ ℝ n H × d model × d model , \displaystyle=(W_{i})_{i=1}^{n_{\rm{H}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{model}}}, (2) 𝒲 ~ \displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{W}} = ( W ~ i ⊤ ) i = 1 n H ∈ ℝ n H × d model × d model . \displaystyle=(\widetilde{W}_{i}^{\top})_{i=1}^{n_{\rm{H}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{model}}}. (3) For both 𝒲 \mathcal{W} and 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} the first mode is referred to as the head mode. For 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , the second and third modes correspond to the query and key computations. For 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} , the second and third modes correspond to the output and value computations. We stack the transpose of W ~ i \widetilde{W}_{i} in ( 3 ) for notational convenience; the key and value modes, which are often treated similarly, now align to the third mode. To reformulate the MHA formula for these tensor-valued weights, we define ℋ ( 1 ) ​ ( X ) := \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{(1)}(X):=\, σ ⁡ ( 𝒲 × 2 X × 3 X d H ) ∈ ℝ n H × N × N , \displaystyle\sigma\left(\frac{\mathcal{W}\times_{2}X\times_{3}X}{\sqrt{d_{\rm{H}}}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times N\times N}\,, (4) ℋ ( 2 ) ​ ( X ) := \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{(2)}(X):=\, 𝒲 ~ × 3 X ∈ ℝ n H × d model × N . \displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}\times_{3}X\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times d_{\rm{model}}\times N}\,. (5) Here, ℋ ( 1 ) \mathcal{H}^{(1)} collects the N × N N\times N attention matrices across all heads, while ℋ ( 2 ) \mathcal{H}^{(2)} collects the projected value representations. The MHA output is then recovered by contracting these tensors over the head and sequence dimensions: MHA ​ ( X , 𝒲 , 𝒲 ~ ) j ​ k = ∑ i , ℓ ℋ i ​ j ​ ℓ ( 1 ) ​ ( X , 𝒲 ) ​ ℋ i ​ k ​ ℓ ( 2 ) ​ ( X , 𝒲 ~ ) . \displaystyle\text{MHA}(X;\mathcal{W},\widetilde{\mathcal{W}})_{jk}=\sum_{i,\ell}\mathcal{H}^{(1)}_{ij\ell}(X;\mathcal{W})\mathcal{H}^{(2)}_{ik\ell}(X;\widetilde{\mathcal{W}})\,. (6) 2.1 Tucker Attention We now aim to find a formulation that enables us to further leverage shared information, e.g., when the column or row space of W i W_{i} or W ~ i \widetilde{W}_{i} shares the same basis over different heads i i . The natural framework for capturing such shared structure is the Tucker decomposition, which factorizes a tensor into a compact core and a set of basis matrices along each mode. This motivates the following definition. Definition 2.1 (Tucker Attention) . Let 𝒲 ∈ ℝ n H × d model × d model \mathcal{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{model}}} and 𝒲 ~ ∈ ℝ n H × d model × d model \widetilde{\mathcal{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{model}}} denote the pre-softmax and post-softmax attention tensors from ( 2 )–( 3 ). Tucker Attention parametrizes these tensors via Tucker decompositions: 𝒲 = 𝒞 × j = 1 3 U j , 𝒲 ~ = 𝒞 ~ × j = 1 3 U ~ j , \displaystyle\mathcal{W}=\mathcal{C}\bigtimes_{j=1}^{3}U_{j},\qquad\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}=\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}\bigtimes_{j=1}^{3}\widetilde{U}_{j}, (7) where 𝒞 ∈ ℝ r 1 × r 2 × r 3 \mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\rm{1}}\times r_{\rm{2}}\times r_{\rm{3}}} and 𝒞 ~ ∈ ℝ r ~ 1 × r ~ 2 × r ~ 3 \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\widetilde{r}_{\rm{1}}\times\widetilde{r}_{\rm{2}}\times\widetilde{r}_{\rm{3}}} are learnable core tensors, and U 1 ∈ ℝ n H × r 1 U_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times r_{\rm{1}}} , U 2 ∈ ℝ d model × r 2 U_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times r_{\rm{2}}} , U 3 ∈ ℝ d model × r 3 U_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times r_{\rm{3}}} (analogously for U ~ 1 , 2 , 3 \widetilde{U}_{1,2,3} ) are learnable basis matrices. The Tucker ranks ( r 1 , r 2 , r 3 ) (r_{\rm{1}},r_{\rm{2}},r_{\rm{3}}) and ( r ~ 1 , r ~ 2 , r ~ 3 ) (\widetilde{r}_{\rm{1}},\widetilde{r}_{\rm{2}},\widetilde{r}_{\rm{3}}) control compression along the head, query/output, and key/value modes, respectively. Attention is computed via ( 6 ). The basis matrices U 2 , U 3 U_{2},U_{3} (resp. U ~ 2 , U ~ 3 \widetilde{U}_{2},\widetilde{U}_{3} ) capture shared subspaces across heads in the query/key (resp. output/value computations), while U 1 U_{1} and U ~ 1 \widetilde{U}_{1} enable compression across the head mode itself. This capability is absent in MHA, GQA, and MLA. Tucker Attention is both expressive and informative to parameter efficient attention. We provide an overview to each of these properties below. Expressivity Tucker Attention is expressive in that state-of-the-art attention methods such as MQA, GQA, and MLA are special cases of Tucker Attention with specific ranks. The key ingredient to this claim is showing, see Theorem B.2 , that 𝒲 \mathcal{W} in ( 2 ) admits the following Tucker factorization: 𝒲 = 𝒞 × 2 W Q Π × 3 W K Π \mathcal{W}=\mathcal{C}\times_{2}W^{\rm{Q}}\Pi\times_{3}W^{\rm{K}}\Pi (8) where Π \Pi is a column permutation matrix. Therefore, low-rank factorizations of W Q W^{\rm{Q}} and W K W^{\rm{K}} directly infer the Tucker ranks of 𝒲 \mathcal{W} . Since MQA, GQA, and MLA all apply a specified low-rank factorization to all/some of the key W K W^{\rm{K}} , query W Q W^{\rm{Q}} , and value W V W^{\rm{V}} matrices, the Tucker ranks of 𝒲 \mathcal{W} and 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} for these methods are as follows: • MHA – 𝒲 \mathcal{W} & 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} : ( n H , d model , d model ) ({n_{\rm{H}}},d_{\rm{model}},d_{\rm{model}}) • MQA – 𝒲 \mathcal{W} & 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} : ( n H , d model , d H ) ({n_{\rm{H}}},d_{\rm{model}},d_{\rm{H}}) • GQA – 𝒲 \mathcal{W} & 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} : ( n H , d model , d H ​ n KV ) ({n_{\rm{H}}},d_{\rm{model}},d_{\rm{H}}n_{\rm{KV}}) , where n KV n_{\rm{KV}} is the number of GQA KV heads. • MLA – 𝒲 \mathcal{W} : ( n H , d c Q , d c K ) ({n_{\rm{H}}},d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}},d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}}) , 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} : ( n H , d model , d c K ) ({n_{\rm{H}}},d_{\rm{model}},d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}}) , where d c K d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}} is the latent dimension for the key and value heads, and d c Q d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}} is the latent dimension for the query heads. Figure 1 illustrates the low-rank representations and contraction modes of the canonical approximate attention mechanisms, where MQA is the special case of GQA with n KV = 1 n_{\rm{KV}}=1 KV heads. Section 2.2 provides a brief overview of MQA, GQA, and MLA and a motivation for the above ranks. A more formal theory is presented in Section B.1 . Informed Compression Across All Modes By viewing parameter reduction through Tucker factorization, Tucker Attention enables compression along all tensor modes: head, query, key, value, and output. This exposes compression opportunities in the head and output modes that MQA, GQA, and MLA leave unexploited by construction. To validate that such compressible structure exists in practice, we perform a post-hoc singular value analysis of the attention tensors 𝒲 \mathcal{W} and 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} from fully trained GPT-2 models (see Section 4.2 for training details). For each mode, we compute the matricization and plot the normalized singular spectrum in Figure 5 (Appendix), with the head mode shown in Figure 2 . The analysis reveals three key findings. First, MHA exhibits similar spectral decay across all modes ( Figures 5(c) , 5(d) , 5(e) and 5(f) ), yet GQA and MLA do not compress the output mode thereby retaining parameters that could be removed. Second, while GQA uses shared heads for the key and value projections, any low-rank behavior in the head mode is lost once the query and output projections are applied (see Figures 5(a) and 5(b) ). Last, Figure 2 shows that MLA and Tucker Attention (with r 1 = 8 r_{\rm{1}}=8 ) exhibit similar low-rank structure in the head mode, but MLA’s parametrization cannot exploit this redundancy. Only through the Tucker lens can this head-mode compression be realized. We claim that Tucker Attention realizes the low-rank tendencies shown above into quantifiable parameter reduction. In Table 1 , we specify the parameter count for training and inference of MHA, MQA, GQA, MLA, and Tucker Attention. The inference costs are calculated post fusing components (for MLA) for additional savings. For a clear presentation, we only consider the case of Tucker Attention where the key, query, value, and output ranks are equal to a given rank r r , and the head ranks pre- and post-softmax are r 1 r_{\rm{1}} . The results show that the parameter count of all methods except Tucker Attention scale as 𝒪 ⁡ ( d model 2 ) \mathcal{O}(d_{\rm{model}}^{2}) while Tucker Attention, by compressing in the output mode, scales as 𝒪 ⁡ ( r ​ d model + r 1 ​ r 2 ) \mathcal{O}(rd_{\rm{model}}+r_{1}r^{2}) . Therefore, if we assume r ≪ d model r\ll d_{\rm{model}} , we expect savings in Tucker Attention over all other approaches without a significant decrease in validation metrics (see Section 4 for validation metric details). Figure 5 suggests that for GPT2 training, assumption r ≪ d model r\ll d_{\rm{model}} is true, and the results in Section 4 indicate that the low-rank ansatz does not harm performance. Figure 2 : Normalized singular spectrum of pre-softmax head mode, Mat 1 ⁡ ( 𝒲 ) \Mat_{1}(\mathcal{W}) , for GPT2 pretraining. See Figure 5 for a detailed description. MLA shares a similar low-rank behavior across heads as Tucker Attention, but is not able to leverage this fact to reduce parameters. We assume d = n H ​ d H d={n_{\rm{H}}}d_{\rm{H}} for MHA, MQA, GQA, n KV n_{\rm{KV}} is the number of kv heads for GQA, d c d_{\rm{c}} is the latent dim/rank of MLA, and ( r 1 , r , r ) (r_{\rm{1}},r,r) are the Tucker ranks of 𝒲 \mathcal{W} and 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} in Tucker Attention. In this discussion, we only focus on the ranks of the above methods with respect to pre-softmax compression, i.e., 𝒲 \mathcal{W} in ( 2 ). The post-softmax ranks for 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} and a more complete theory are found in Section B.1 . Our discussion investigates the rank of W Q W^{\rm{Q}} and W K W^{\rm{K}} of different attention mechanisms and concludes the Tucker ranks using Theorem B.2 . 2.2.1 Multi and Group Query Attention Group query attention with selects n KV n_{\rm{KV}} K heads W i K W^{\rm{K}}_{i} (and analogously V heads), each of size d model × d H d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{H}} , see Figure 1(b) . Therefore, W K W^{\rm{K}} has a maximum rank of n KV ​ d H n_{\rm{KV}}d_{\rm{H}} . A similar shared compression technique is applied to the value heads. Thus the ranks in the key and value modes of 𝒲 \mathcal{W} and 𝒲 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{W}} are at most n KV ​ d H n_{\rm{KV}}d_{\rm{H}} . We view MQA as the special case of GQA with n KV = 1 n_{\rm{KV}}=1 . 2.2.2 Multihead Latent Attention In the case of MLA, the key heads are factorized as W i K = W DKV ​ W i UK W^{\rm{K}}_{i}=W^{\rm{DKV}}W^{\rm{UK}}_{i} , where W DKV ∈ ℝ d model × d c K W^{\rm{DKV}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}}} projects inputs into the latent space of dimension d c K d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}} and W i K W^{\rm{K}}_{i} prolongs the inputs up into the head-specific ambient space. Defining W UK = [ W 1 UK , ⋯ , W n H UK ] ∈ ℝ d c Q × d model W^{\rm{UK}}=[W^{\rm{UK}}_{1},\cdots,W^{\rm{UK}}_{n_{\rm{H}}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}}\times d_{\rm{model}}} , we have W K = W DKV ​ W UK W^{\rm{K}}=W^{\rm{DKV}}W^{\rm{UK}} , and it is easy to see that W K W^{\rm{K}} has a rank of d c K d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}} . The query heads are factorized similarly to the key heads, yielding W Q = W DQ ​ W UQ W^{\rm{Q}}=W^{\rm{DQ}}W^{\rm{UQ}} where W DQ ∈ ℝ d model × d c Q W^{\rm{DQ}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}}} , and W Q W^{\rm{Q}} having a rank of d c Q d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}} . Stacking W i UK W^{\rm{UK}}_{i} , respectively W i UQ W^{\rm{UQ}}_{i} , into tensors 𝒲 UK ∈ ℝ n H × d H × d c K \mathcal{W}^{\rm UK}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times d_{\rm{H}}\times d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}}} and 𝒲 UQ ∈ ℝ n H × d H × d c Q \mathcal{W}^{\rm UQ}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{\rm{H}}}\times d_{\rm{H}}\times d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}}} yields the MLA formulation illustrated in Figure 1(c) . It is evident that the two up-projection tensors can be absorbed into the Tucker core of ( 8 ), yielding a more parameter-efficient representation, i.e., the Tucker Attention representation. Lastly, we consider two versions of the value head compression. The first, shared KV , is the standard approach where the down projection W DKV W^{\rm{DKV}} is also used for value heads, i.e., W i V = W DKV ​ W i UV W^{\rm{V}}_{i}=W^{\rm{DKV}}W^{\rm{UV}}_{i} . We also consider the case, called separated KV , where W V W^{\rm{V}} uses its own down projection, i.e., W i V = W DV ​ W i UV W^{\rm{V}}_{i}=W^{\rm{DV}}W^{\rm{UV}}_{i} where W UV ∈ ℝ d model × d c K W^{\rm{UV}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm{model}}\times d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}}} .

sections.heading: 4 Numerical Results
sections.text: In this section, we compare MHA, GQA, MLA and the proposed Tucker Attention parametrization on vision transformers and GPT2. We use the notation for GQA and MLA presented in Section 2.2 . For Tucker Attention, we fix r 1 = r 1 ~ r_{\rm{1}}=\widetilde{r_{\rm{1}}} , r 2 = r 2 ~ r_{\rm{2}}=\widetilde{r_{\rm{2}}} , and r 3 = r 3 ~ r_{\rm{3}}=\widetilde{r_{\rm{3}}} , and present the ranks as ( r 1 , r 2 , r 3 ) (r_{\rm{1}},r_{\rm{2}},r_{\rm{3}}) . 4.1 ViT16b on Cifar10/Cifar100 & ViT32l, ViT16g on ImageNet1k Setup We initialize the model weights 4 4 4 We refrain from full training due to the associated significant computational expense. Full pretraining results can be found in Section 4.2 . from the ViT Huggingface endpoints and train on the corresponding down-stream dataset. The low-rank parameterizations GQA, MLA and Tucker Attention are initialized by SVD-based approximation of the MHA weights; see Section C.1 for details, full training setup and additional tests. Findings Figure 3 reports the mean of 5 5 training runs, with standard deviation of less than 0.1 0.1 % per setup. We observe that the proposed Tucker Attention achieves a significantly better parameter-to-accuracy ratio than GQA and MLA: Tucker Attention requires almost an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters to achieve similar performance than GQA and MLA. We further observe that lowering the ranks r 2 r_{\rm{2}} and r 3 r_{\rm{3}} is more beneficial for Tucker Attention than very low r 1 r_{\rm{1}} ranks, e.g. r 1 ≤ 2 r_{\rm{1}}\leq 2 . We initialize the model from scratch with random weights, fixing the random seed for comparability between methods. We use the same training hyperparameters for all methods, see Section C.2 for details. For each attention mechanism we train GPT2 twice: once equipped with a position embedding vector in the embedding layer and once using RoPE, where we remove the position embedding vector and instead apply RoPE at each pre-softmax attention layer. MHA and GQA setup: Both methods are implemented canonically. MLA setup: Unless noted otherwise, we follow the implementation of ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024 ) for consistency. Thus we train MLA in unfused mode with decoupled RoPE . Tucker Attention setup: We use the parametrization of Equation 7 , and the proposed variation of Section 3.2 . Findings Figure 9 (Appendix) reports the validation loss curve 5 5 5 The training loss curve follows the same structure. of GPT2 with classical position embedding for MHA, GQA ( n KV = 2 n_{\rm{KV}}=2 ), MLA ( d c Q = d c K = 128 d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}}=d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}}=128 ) with shared KV down-projection, and Tucker Attention with ranks ( 8,128 , 64 ) (8,128,64) . In this case, MLA and Tucker Attention have the same KV cache size during inference. We observe that Tucker Attention converges at the same rate as the canonical methods, reaching a lower loss than MLA. Throughout the GPT2 experiments we observed that MLA with shared KV exhibits small instabilities, and even diverges for d c K = d c Q ≤ 128 d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{K}}=d_{\rm{c}}^{\rm{Q}}\leq 128 . Table 2 compares the GPT2 variants’ validation performance on a set of one-shot validation tests, reporting perplexity (lower is better), validation loss (lower is better), and validation accuracy (higher is better), as well as the total number of trainable parameters in the attention layers and the total required KV cache during inference. In the category w/o RoPE, we observe that Tucker Attention with ranks ( 8,128 , 64 ) (8,128,64) requires about 18 18 % of the parameters of MHA and 39 39 % of the MLA parameters to obtain competitive validation results. That is, Tucker Attention achieves the similar mean perplexity and similar mean accuracy as the baseline methods. Similarly, we observe in the second part of the table that Tucker Attention is compatible with latent RoPE, implemented using Equation 12 . Findings A similar trend appears as in the GPT-2 results: Tucker Attention uses only 10–20% of the LLaMA3 baseline (GQA, n KV = 8 n_{\rm{KV}}=8 ), with a modest 1–3% increase in validation cross-entropy loss. It reduces the KV cache by 4–8 × \times , depending on rank. This reduction in parameters and KV cache lowers training cost, decreasing iteration wall time by up to 20% vs. MHA and 15% vs. the GQA ( n KV = 8 n_{\rm{KV}}=8 ) baseline. Additionally, Tucker Attention outperforms MLA in both validation loss and parameter count. We conclude that the introduced viewpoint of treating the pre- and post-softmax weights as one tensor-valued object each yields several practical benefits. The deduced Tucker Attention scheme is more parameter efficient than existing methods, allows introducing latent RoPE, is compatible with KV caching, and combines the memory benefits of MLA and GQA for FlashAttention during training and inference.
